1037.title: Tibet, 1950–1959
1037.hook: Chinese forces entered Tibet; the Dalai Lama left for India, and others followed him into exile
1037.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep their practice in rebuilt monasteries, schools and community centers, and some hold Tibet and all who suffered in their daily prayers and loving-kindness practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Myanmar: monks who walked for their people, and monks who stood against hatred spoken in the robe's name. Your line: the robe for peace. Did a hateful word cross your path, and what did you do with it? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

What would you carry if you had to leave home at night, on foot, over mountains, and you didn't know when you'd come back? A coat. Water. A photograph, maybe. Some Tibetan families who crossed into India and Nepal speak of carrying something else too: a text wrapped in cloth, a small image of the Buddha, a string of prayer beads, a teacher walking a few steps ahead. Today's history isn't one night. It's a long exile, and the practice that went with it.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `A TEXT WRAPPED IN CLOTH.` → `A LONG EXILE.`

segments.voice: In the years named in today's title, Chinese forces entered Tibet, and Tibet came under the government in Beijing. The Chinese government and Tibetans in exile tell those years very differently, and this lesson won't settle that argument. What it can tell is what happened to a community of practice. After unrest in Lhasa, the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetan Buddhists hold as a great teacher, left for India. Others followed, monks and nuns and lay families, walking through high passes. In India, with very little, the exiles rebuilt. Monasteries with the old names rose again in new places, so that a monastery from Tibet might now stand in the hot plains of southern India. Schools taught Tibetan children their language and their texts. Debate courtyards filled again with monks clapping their hands as they argued a point, just as their teachers had. And in his public teaching from exile, the Dalai Lama has returned again and again to compassion, including for those he disagrees with, and he has said that an opponent can be your teacher of patience. The Pali word for that patience is khanti, and the Dhammapada sets it very high. In Max Müller's translation: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance." Patience here doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. Exile still hurts. Homes are still missed. Patience is what lets a person keep the grief without letting it harden into hate, and keep teaching while they wait.
screen: `CHINESE FORCES ENTER TIBET.` · `THE DALAI LAMA LEAVES FOR INDIA.` · `MONASTERIES REBUILT IN EXILE.` · then, large: `PATIENCE, THE HIGHEST PENANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold refugees in metta, loving-kindness. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. First, bring to mind anyone who has had to leave home: Tibetan families, or refugees from anywhere, or someone you know. You don't need faces; a sense of them is enough. With each out-breath, let a simple wish go toward them, in words that feel true to you: may you be safe, may you find a home. If the mind drifts to the news or to blame, notice that, and come back to the wish. Last, widen it to everyone caught up in that history, on every side. The bell holds the time.
Tibet. The high land whose teachers and families carried their practice into exile, and rebuilt it, monastery by monastery, far from home. Today's word.
Your line: the long exile. Today, when you walk through your own front door, pause on the threshold for one breath and remember someone who can't walk through theirs. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

1038.title: Cambodia's killing years
1038.hook: the Khmer Rouge closed the monasteries and killed monks; the sangha was rebuilt from very few
1038.howItsDone: Cambodian Buddhists remember those years at ceremonies for the dead and at the monasteries that were rebuilt, and monks and lay people have kept up walks and gatherings for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tibet, and families who walked into exile and rebuilt their monasteries far from home. Your line: the long exile. Whose doorway did you remember? Day one thousand thirty-eight.

A monk can't ordain himself. In the Theravada tradition, a new monk is received by a gathering of monks who are already ordained, chanting together, so the robe passes from hand to hand in an unbroken line. That line is usually so ordinary nobody thinks about it. Then comes a time when the gathering itself almost disappears. What happens to a tradition when there are hardly enough monks left to make a new one? That is today's history.
screen: `A MONK CAN'T ORDAIN HIMSELF.` → `THE GATHERING RECEIVES HIM.` → `WHAT IF IT VANISHES?`

segments.voice: In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge took power and set out to remake the whole country from nothing. Cities were emptied. Money, schools and markets were abolished. Religion was treated as an enemy of the new order. Monasteries were closed or turned into prisons and storehouses. Monks were forced out of their robes, sent to labor in the fields, and killed. Old palm-leaf texts were burned or left to rot. It is hard to say how much was lost. When the regime fell, the sangha, the community of monks, had to be rebuilt from the few who were left, including monks who had survived by hiding, or in exile, or by putting the robe aside. Ordinations began again. Monasteries reopened, sometimes in buildings that still bore the marks of what had been done there. One monk who survived abroad, Maha Ghosananda, came home and led peace walks across the country, with monks, nuns and lay people walking side by side through places still scarred by war. He taught that peace is made the way a walk is made, step by step, and that each step can be a meditation. Walking for peace through those places, after those years, was not a pleasant gesture. It was a hard choice about what to rebuild. And the rebuilding shows this: a line of practice can come close to breaking and still continue. The gathering grew again, one ordination at a time, until there were monks enough to receive the next.
screen: `MONASTERIES CLOSED, MONKS DISROBED.` · `REBUILT FROM THE FEW WHO WERE LEFT.` · `MAHA GHOSANANDA'S PEACE WALKS.` · then, large: `ONE ORDINATION AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor a rebuilt community. Sit and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind a community that was broken and came back: Cambodia's monasteries, or a congregation after a fire, a neighborhood after a flood, a family after a hard year. Picture the first few people who showed up again, before anyone knew it would work. With each in-breath, notice their courage. With each out-breath, offer them thanks. If grief comes up for what was lost, let it be there; it belongs in this too. The bell holds the time.
Cambodia's killing years. The time when the sangha was nearly destroyed, and the few who were left began to receive new monks again. Today's word.

Your line: rebuilt from few. Today, look for one thing near you that someone started again after it broke, a shop, a garden, a friendship, and say thank you for it, out loud or quietly. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

1039.title: Saigon, 1963
1039.hook: the monk Thich Quang Duc died in protest against the persecution of Buddhists; told with care, never as an example
1039.howItsDone: Vietnamese Buddhist communities remember Thich Quang Duc at memorial services, and some teachers who speak of him frame his death within the protest's call to end suffering, not as something to imitate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cambodia, and a sangha rebuilt one ordination at a time. Your line: rebuilt from few. What did you thank today that someone had started again? Day one thousand thirty-nine.

Before anything else today, a word about how this story is told. It involves a death, and it is a hard story. It's told here so that you know it, not so that anyone copies it. If you are carrying thoughts of harming yourself today, please pause this lesson and reach out to someone near you, or to a local crisis line. You matter more than any lesson. Now, a city street, and a protest that the world saw.
screen: `A HARD STORY, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `NOT AN EXAMPLE.` → `IF YOU'RE HURTING, REACH OUT.`

segments.voice: In South Vietnam, Buddhists were protesting against the government of the day. They said they were being treated unfairly: limits on flying the Buddhist flag, arrests, and violence against those who gathered. Monks and nuns marched and fasted and held vigils. Then, at a busy crossroads in Saigon, a monk named Thich Quang Duc sat down in the meditation posture and ended his own life, as a protest. A photograph of that moment went around the world, and the pressure on the government grew. Here is where care matters. Buddhist teachers have not agreed about how to understand what he did. The first precept of Buddhist ethics is to abstain from taking life, and some teachers include one's own life in that. Some have described his act as a self-offering, made out of compassion, to draw the world's eyes to suffering. Others have said that, whatever his intention, it should never be repeated, and they have mourned it as a loss. Both kinds of voices honor the man; they read his death differently. What the accounts share is the suffering around it: people who were afraid to practice their faith openly, and a protest meant to make the world look. So the lesson isn't the act. The lesson is the suffering that came before it, and the way monks, nuns and lay people kept protesting, with marches, fasts and vigils. To tell this story with care is to keep both in view: the courage people saw, and the life that ended.
screen: `BUDDHISTS PROTEST UNFAIR TREATMENT.` · `A MONK'S PROTEST AT A CROSSROADS.` · `TEACHERS READ IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `KEEP THE SUFFERING IN VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold the suffering gently. Sit, and rest one hand on your chest if that's comfortable. Feel it rise and fall. Bring to mind the people in this story: those who were afraid to gather, the monk, the people who watched, the families. You don't have to understand everything. Just let compassion, karuna, touch it, the way you'd hold something fragile. If it feels heavy, come back to the hand on your chest and the breath beneath it. Gentle is enough. The bell holds the time.
Saigon. The city where Buddhists protested their treatment, and where a monk's death drew the world's attention, a story told with care and never held up as an example. Today's word.
Your line: told with care. Today, if a hard story comes up in conversation or on a screen, slow down before you pass it on, and ask whether you're telling it with care. Day one thousand thirty-nine.

1040.title: Mongolia's monasteries
1040.hook: monasteries were torn down and monks killed; years later, practice returned
1040.howItsDone: Mongolian Buddhists visit rebuilt monasteries to make offerings, light butter lamps and ask monks for blessings, and some families still keep images and texts their relatives once hid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saigon, a hard story about protest and loss. Your line: told with care. Did you slow down before passing on a hard story? Day one thousand forty.

On the open grasslands of Mongolia, there are places where only foundations show in the grass: a line of stones, a raised floor, a scatter of broken tile. Herders ride past them. Some of those lines of stone were once monasteries, with courtyards, chanting halls and young monks learning their texts. Today's history asks two questions. How does a monastery disappear? And how, years later, does practice come back to a place that had almost forgotten it?
screen: `STONES IN THE GRASS.` → `ONCE A MONASTERY.` → `HOW DOES PRACTICE COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Buddhism had long been woven into Mongolian life, in the Tibetan form of the tradition, with monasteries large and small across the country. Then, under a communist government closely tied to the Soviet Union, a campaign turned against it. Monasteries were torn down or emptied. Monks were arrested and killed, or forced to return to lay life and marry. Statues were melted, and texts were burned. Yet even then, some things were hidden. Families buried images in the ground or kept a text hidden at the back of a chest. Some former monks kept the chants alive in their heads, saying them quietly at home. When the government changed, the doors opened again. Old monks who still remembered the ceremonies began teaching young ones. Monasteries were rebuilt, sometimes on the old foundations, and people came back to make offerings and ask for blessings. The return wasn't neat. Teachers had to be found, texts recovered, a whole way of training started again almost from memory. But it happened. The Dhammapada has a pair of verses that fit those quiet years. A person who can recite a great deal of the teaching but doesn't live it, it says, is like a cowherd counting other people's cows. And a person who can recite only a little, but lives it, letting go of greed, hatred and delusion, has a real share in the life of a renunciant. An old monk in a back room, saying a few remembered lines under his breath, was not counting anyone's cows. A little, kept and lived, was enough to start again.
screen: `A CAMPAIGN AGAINST THE MONASTERIES.` · `IMAGES BURIED, CHANTS REMEMBERED.` · `OLD MONKS TEACH YOUNG ONES.` · then, large: `A LITTLE, KEPT AND LIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor a return. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Rest your attention on the breath at the belly. Sooner or later the mind will wander off, to a plan, a worry, a song. That isn't failure. The moment you notice and come back is a small return, the same shape as a chant remembered after long silence. Each time, say silently, back, and begin again with the next breath. Don't count the returns or judge them. Let each one be welcome. The bell holds the time.
Mongolia's monasteries. Torn down in a campaign against religion, remembered in hidden texts and quiet chants, and rebuilt when the doors opened again. Today's word.
Your line: it returned. Today, notice one thing that comes back to you, the breath, a song, an old habit of kindness, and when it does, say quietly to yourself, it returned. Day one thousand forty.

1041.title: China's Cultural Revolution
1041.hook: temples were closed and monks sent away; since then, the doors have reopened
1041.howItsDone: In reopened temples in China, lay Buddhists offer incense, bow before the Buddha images and join chanting services, and monks and nuns again train novices under the rules that now govern religious life there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mongolia's monasteries: buried images, remembered chants, and old monks teaching young ones. Your line: it returned. What came back to you yesterday? Day one thousand forty-one.

A temple door is heavy, often painted red, with rows of round studs and a high wooden threshold you step over rather than on. In the mornings a monk swings it open, and in the evenings it closes. For a stretch of years in China, temple doors stayed shut, some with a chain across them. Today is about what happened behind those doors, and about the morning they began to open again.
screen: `A HEAVY RED DOOR.` → `SHUT, WITH A CHAIN.` → `THE MORNING IT OPENED.`

segments.voice: The Cultural Revolution was a political campaign in China, launched by Mao Zedong, that set out to sweep away what it called old ideas, old customs, old culture and old habits. Other religions came under attack too, not Buddhism alone. Young Red Guards entered temples, smashed statues and burned scriptures. Temples were closed, or turned into factories, schools and storehouses. Monks and nuns were sent away to labor, made to return to lay life, and some were beaten or killed. For years, practicing openly could be dangerous. People who lived through it tell of a statue walled up behind plaster, and of the Buddha's name said under the breath at home. When the campaign ended and policy changed, temples began to reopen. Statues were repaired or carved again. Some monks who had survived returned to their old monasteries, gray now, and began to train new novices. Religious life in China today still runs under government rules, and people inside and outside the country describe those rules very differently. But the doors did reopen, and there are temples busy again with incense and chanting. There's a verse for the people who kept steady through it. The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's translation, "As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise." The campaign was a great wind of blame. Some people, quietly, did not falter. And the temples stand open now partly because of what they kept.
screen: `A CAMPAIGN AGAINST THE OLD.` · `TEMPLES CLOSED, STATUES SMASHED.` · `HIDDEN BEHIND PLASTER.` · then, large: `A SOLID ROCK IN THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: visit or picture a reopened temple. If there's a temple near you, you might go another day. For now, picture one. See the heavy door swing open. Step over the threshold. Smell the incense. Hear a bell somewhere inside, and the low sound of chanting. Notice the people: an old woman lighting a stick of incense, a monk sweeping, a family with a child. Let yourself simply be glad the door is open. When the mind wanders, come back to the doorway and step through again. The bell holds the time.
China's Cultural Revolution. The campaign that closed temples and sent monks and nuns away, and after which, slowly, the doors reopened. Today's word.
Your line: the doors reopened. Today, every time you open a door, notice it for one breath, and remember the temple doors that were chained and then swung open again. Day one thousand forty-one.

1042.title: Bamiyan remembered
1042.hook: the empty niches in the cliff where the great Buddhas stood
1042.howItsDone: Buddhists and others remember Bamiyan in talks, exhibitions and visits to the valley, and the question of whether to rebuild the statues or leave the niches empty is still discussed among scholars, local people and heritage bodies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, China's Cultural Revolution, and temple doors chained shut that swung open again. Your line: the doors reopened. Which door did you notice? Day one thousand forty-two.

A tall arch is cut deep into a honey-colored cliff. It's the shape of a standing figure, but there's no figure in it. Just rock, scarred and hollow, with small caves dotted around it where people once lived and prayed. Farther along the same cliff, another arch, another emptiness. Down below, in the valley, fields and poplar trees, and children walking to school. The cliff is in Afghanistan, in the valley of Bamiyan. Today we sit with what used to stand there.
screen: `AN ARCH IN THE CLIFF.` → `NO FIGURE IN IT.` → `THE VALLEY OF BAMIYAN.`

segments.voice: Long ago, great standing Buddhas were carved into that cliff, giant figures in their niches, looking out over a valley that lay along old trade routes. Buddhist monks lived in the caves around them, and travelers and pilgrims passed through and wrote about what they saw. Long after the valley's people had become Muslim, the statues stayed, part of the landscape and of local memory. Then the Taliban government of the time declared them idols and destroyed them with explosives. People from around the world and from different faiths, Muslims among them, spoke out against it. What was left were the empty niches. Since then there has been a long debate about what to do. Some want to rebuild the Buddhas. Some say the empty niches should stay as they are, as a witness to what happened. Others have tried light: once, an image of a Buddha was projected into an empty niche. Bamiyan raises a Buddhist question in a sharp way. What is lost when a statue is lost? Images of the Buddha are deeply honored; people bow to them, offer flowers, and some speak of feeling the Buddha near. And yet the old texts tell of a monk named Vakkali, sick and near death, who longed just to look at the Buddha's body one more time. When the Buddha came to his bedside, he asked what good it would do to see this decaying body, and said that whoever sees the teaching sees him, and whoever sees him sees the teaching. So the niches can be read two ways at once. They are a real loss, and grief for them makes sense. And they are a reminder that what the statues pointed to, the teaching, did not fall with the stone.
screen: `GREAT BUDDHAS IN THE CLIFF.` · `DESTROYED, LEAVING EMPTY NICHES.` · `REBUILD, OR LEAVE THEM EMPTY?` · then, large: `THE TEACHING DID NOT FALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: sit with an empty space. Find one near you: an empty chair, a doorway, the space between your hands, or the quiet room around you. Rest your eyes on it, or close them and feel it. Don't fill it. Notice the urge to fill it, with a thought, a plan, a song, and let the urge pass. If something you've lost comes to mind, let it sit in the empty space with you for a while. The emptiness can hold grief and calm at once. The bell holds the time.
Bamiyan remembered. The valley in Afghanistan where great Buddhas stood in the cliff, and where the empty niches still remind people of what was there. Today's word.
Your line: the empty niches. Today, when you notice an empty space, a chair, a shelf, a gap in a conversation, let it stay empty for one breath before you fill it. Day one thousand forty-two.

1043.title: Conversion and caste
1043.hook: the Ambedkarite movement today, and Buddhism as a path of dignity in India
1043.howItsDone: Ambedkarite Buddhists gather at neighborhood viharas and community halls, take the refuges and precepts together, read Ambedkar's writings in study circles, greet one another with "Jai Bhim", and some return each year to the ground in Nagpur where he took refuge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bamiyan, and two empty niches in a cliff. Your line: the empty niches. Did you let an empty space stay empty for a breath? Day one thousand forty-three, the end of a hard week.

"Jai Bhim." In parts of India, that's how some Buddhists greet each other: victory to Bhim. Bhim is Bhimrao Ambedkar, and his portrait hangs beside the Buddha's in some homes and community halls, and on banners at gatherings. He wears a suit and glasses and holds a book. To understand why a lawyer in a suit sits next to the Buddha, you need today's story, about birth, about dignity, and about a choice a whole movement made.
screen: `JAI BHIM.` → `A PORTRAIT BESIDE THE BUDDHA.` → `BIRTH AND DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: There's a scene in the old texts that fits today. A brahmin tending his sacred fire sees the Buddha coming on his alms round and shouts at him to stop where he is, calling him an outcast. The Buddha doesn't defend his own family. He asks whether the man even knows what an outcast is, or what makes one. Then he answers: no one is an outcast by birth, and no one is a brahmin by birth. It is deeds that make a person either. That is the Vasala Sutta, and the Dhammapada says much the same. As this path told some weeks ago, B. R. Ambedkar, born into a community treated as untouchable, took refuge in the Buddha with a great crowd in Nagpur. Today his followers carry that choice into ordinary places. Small viharas stand in city neighborhoods and villages, his portrait beside the Buddha's. Study circles read his book, The Buddha and His Dhamma. Some families take the refuges and precepts together at weddings and naming ceremonies. Each year, on the anniversary, crowds return to the ground in Nagpur. And you'll hear a call of his repeated at gatherings: educate, agitate, organize. For many in the movement, dignity means schooling, work and fair treatment as well as the refuges, and some describe Buddhism as the path that gave all of it a name. People of other traditions in India, Hindus among them, have also worked against caste; this story isn't a contest between faiths. It is the story of people told by birth that they were less, who now greet each other with two words: Jai Bhim. And a look back at this week: Tibet in exile, Cambodia rebuilt, Saigon told with care, Mongolia and China reopening, Bamiyan's empty niches, and today, a path chosen for dignity. A hard week of history, and every day, something kept.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: honor someone's dignity. Sit and settle with a few breaths. Bring to mind someone people tend to overlook: the person who cleans the building, the one who collects the trash, a neighbor others talk past. See their face if you can. With each in-breath, notice that they have a whole life, as full as yours. With each out-breath, wish them well. Then, if you'd like, plan one small thing: learn their name, or use it, or thank them properly next time. The bell holds the time.
